title: Git workflow
summary: How a change moves from a branch to the default branch: branch names, working on the default branch, Refs trailers, whether a plan is delivered per step or as one pull request, and the fixed rules of Conventional Commit subjects, squash merge and green CI.

questions.prompt: Which regular expression must a branch name match? (default: a Conventional Commit type, a slash, then a slug)
How is the default branch protected from direct work?

options.label: A git hook and CI refuse work on it, with an instruction elsewhere
options.tradeoff: A commit or push on the default branch fails before it leaves the machine; a release step that needs it must be allowed by name.

options.label: Instruction only
options.tradeoff: Nothing refuses it; depends on the agent following the rule, and on the platform's own branch protection.

questions.prompt: Must commits carry a Refs trailer?

options.label: Encouraged, not enforced
options.tradeoff: The attribute skill proposes trailers and the PR description lists them; no hook fails a commit without one. Works with or without a knowledge base.

options.label: Required on every commit
options.tradeoff: Every commit is traceable, but a commit with nothing to reference (a typo fix) needs a reference anyway, and a project without a knowledge base has nothing to point at.

options.label: Not used
options.tradeoff: No trailer convention and nothing to maintain; commits are not linked to decisions.

questions.prompt: How is a plan delivered: one pull request per step, or one for the whole plan?

options.label: One branch and pull request per plan step, merged on green before its issue closes
options.tradeoff: Small reviews, a step's issue closes as it lands, and steps marked as parallel can run side by side in separate worktrees; a plan of many steps makes many pull requests.

options.label: One branch and one pull request for the whole plan, one commit per step
options.tradeoff: One review and one merge for the plan, but a large diff, steps run one after another on one branch, a failure late in the plan holds back the steps before it, and the branch needs a rebase if the default branch moves under it.

decisions.title: Branches are named {{answer.branch-pattern}}
decisions.body:
## Decision

A branch name matches `{{answer.branch-pattern}}`, and the name identifies the change (pack {{pack.id}}@{{pack.version}}).

## Why

A change is one branch and one pull request, so the name is how the change is found again.

decisions.title: One change is one branch and one pull request
decisions.body:
## Decision

A change is one branch and one pull request, and the slug of the branch is the change id. Commits follow Conventional Commits; the pull request is squash merged once CI is green (pack {{pack.id}}@{{pack.version}}).

## Why

A stable change id lets tools that track changes (a spec tool, a changelog) match a change to its branch and pull request.

guardrails.title: Branch names must match the project pattern

frontmatter.derivation-note: Given a change is one branch and one pull request, the branch name identifies the change, so a name that does not match the pattern cannot be traced to its type or slug.

enforcement.check: The current branch, or the pull request head in CI, matches the pattern
Name a new branch `type/slug` before the first commit

guardrails.body:
## Guardrail

A branch is named `{{answer.branch-pattern}}` (by default `type/slug`: a Conventional Commit type, a slash, and the change id). The default branch is exempt here and protected by its own rule.

guardrails.title: Commit subjects must follow Conventional Commits

frontmatter.derivation-note: Given changelogs and release notes are generated from commit type prefixes, a non-conforming subject silently drops out of them.

enforcement.check: Every non-merge commit not yet on the default branch has a Conventional Commits subject

guardrails.body:
## Guardrail

Commit subjects use `type(scope)?: summary` with a Conventional Commits type. Write them with the `attribute` skill where the project has it.

guardrails.title: A change lands as one squashed pull request with green CI

frontmatter.derivation-note: Given one change is one branch and one pull request, the history keeps one commit per change only if the merge squashes, and a red pull request must not merge.

enforcement.check: Merge a pull request only when its CI checks pass, and squash it into one commit on the default branch

guardrails.body:
## Guardrail

Open one pull request per branch. Merge it by squash, and only once its CI checks pass. Advisory (tier 1): nothing enforces it; hosting-platform settings (required checks, merge queue) are the project's to configure and go-getter cannot write them.

procedures.title: Work a change from branch to merge
procedures.body:
## Procedure

1. Start from the default branch and create a branch named for the change: `git switch -c <type>/<slug>`.
2. Commit with a Conventional Commit subject (`type: summary`) and a body that says why.
3. Before the pull request, do the preparation yourself: run the project's knowledge capture, conformance and lint checks and write the commit message and description, then fix what they find. Hand a person only gated actions (an approval, a write a guardrail gates), each as one question through the host's question tool where it has one, never a list of steps for them to do.
4. Push the branch and open one pull request for it.
5. When CI is green, squash merge the pull request and delete the branch.
6. After `go-getter ship` confirms the merge, it removes the task's worktree from the main checkout when the remote branch is gone or the branch or its pull request is merged, and nothing is uncommitted (the rule of `go-getter worktree clean`); it keeps the local branch and prints the main checkout path, where you continue. Gitignored files in a removed worktree are deleted with it. `go-getter plan start --worktree` at the concurrency limit runs the same clean once and retries once before refusing; that clean can remove a worktree whose remote branch is gone even if another session still uses it, so finish or push work before its branch is merged or closed.

decisions.title: The default branch takes no direct work
decisions.body:
## Decision

A git hook and CI refuse a commit or push while the default branch is checked out, and agents are told the same (pack {{pack.id}}@{{pack.version}}).

## Why

Every change goes through a branch and a pull request, so review and CI see it before the default branch does.

guardrails.title: Work must not happen on the default branch

frontmatter.derivation-note: Given every change goes through a branch and a pull request, a commit or push on the default branch skips review and CI.

enforcement.check: The current branch, or the pull request head in CI, is not the default branch
Never commit or push to the default branch; create a `type/slug` branch first

guardrails.body:
## Guardrail

Never commit or push on the default branch; work on a branch and open a pull request. A git hook refuses a commit on the default branch and a push of it: before a push the refs being pushed decide, so a tag or another branch may go from any checkout and `git push origin feat:main` is refused.

decisions.title: Work on the default branch is discouraged by instruction only
decisions.body:
## Decision

Agents are told not to commit or push on the default branch; nothing refuses it (pack {{pack.id}}@{{pack.version}}).

## Why

The project accepted the risk for less machinery, or relies on the platform's branch protection.

guardrails.title: Work must not happen on the default branch

frontmatter.derivation-note: Given every change goes through a branch and a pull request, a commit or push on the default branch skips review and CI.

enforcement.check: Never commit or push to the default branch; create a `type/slug` branch first

guardrails.body:
## Guardrail

Never commit or push on the default branch; work on a branch and open a pull request. Advisory: nothing refuses it. A push from another branch to the default branch's name (`git push origin feat:main`) is not detected.

decisions.title: Refs trailers are encouraged
decisions.body:
## Decision

Commits link the decisions, facts and guardrails they implement with `Refs:` trailers, proposed by the attribute skill and listed in the pull request; nothing fails a commit without one (pack {{pack.id}}@{{pack.version}}).

## Why

A `Refs:` trailer links a commit to the decision, fact or guardrail it implements, so the reason for a change can be found from the code.

decisions.title: Refs trailers are required
decisions.body:
## Decision

Every commit carries a `Refs:` trailer naming the artifact it implements (pack {{pack.id}}@{{pack.version}}).

## Why

A `Refs:` trailer links a commit to the decision, fact or guardrail it implements, so the reason for a change can be found from the code.

guardrails.title: Every commit must carry a Refs trailer

frontmatter.derivation-note: Given the project requires every commit to be traceable to a decision, fact or guardrail, a commit without a trailer breaks that link.

enforcement.check: Every non-merge commit not yet on the default branch has a Refs trailer

guardrails.body:
## Guardrail

Every commit message ends with at least one `Refs: <path>` trailer. Write it with the `attribute` skill where the project has it.

decisions.title: Refs trailers are not used
decisions.body:
## Decision

Commits carry no `Refs:` trailers (pack {{pack.id}}@{{pack.version}}).

## Why

A `Refs:` trailer links a commit to the decision, fact or guardrail it implements, so the reason for a change can be found from the code.

decisions.title: A plan is delivered one pull request per step
decisions.body:
## Decision

Each step of a plan is its own change: a branch named for the step, one pull request, merged by squash once CI is green, after which the step's issue closes. Steps marked as parallel with no shared files may run at the same time, each in its own worktree. `go-getter ship` takes a step from working tree to merge (pack {{pack.id}}@{{pack.version}}).

## Why

Small pull requests are reviewed and reverted one at a time, and the plan's status follows the merged state of its issues.

decisions.title: A plan is delivered as one pull request for the whole plan
decisions.body:
## Decision

A plan is one change: one branch named `feat/` plus the plan's file name, one commit per step with the step marked done in the plan file in the same commit, and one pull request opened with `go-getter pr` once the plan is done and merged with `go-getter ship`. Steps run one after another on that branch. The steps' issues close after the merge, with the usual approval (pack {{pack.id}}@{{pack.version}}).

## Why

The project prefers one review and one merge for a plan over many small ones, and accepts a larger diff, a late failure holding back earlier steps, and a rebase when the default branch moves.
